implementation_notes: No language can tell you that a supplier dependency exists; the detection is a boundary review, and it is cheap if it is habitual. Enumerate every external dependency the application calls directly — storage, identity, queue, model provider, payment gateway, cloud primitives — and for each record the surface actually used: which APIs, which data formats, which proprietary language, and whether any business rule is expressed inside the supplier. Each entry is one switching cost, ranked by how much of the domain depends on it. The structural fix is uniform: declare an interface in your own vocabulary at the boundary, adapt the supplier to it, and keep the supplier's types out of the domain entirely. Nothing in the abstraction is vendor-specific, which is precisely why it stays put when the supplier changes.
idiom_name: seam at every supplier-facing edge (facade / adapter / published language)
code_sketch:
# before: the supplier's vocabulary is the domain's vocabulary
db.execute("SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE created_at > ?", cutoff)

# after: the rule is yours, the supplier is behind a port
interface Ledger { Money: total_since(Instant) }   # your vocabulary
class SqlLedger(Ledger):                        # the seam = the strike price
    def total_since(self, since): return self.db.sum(where='created_at > ?', args=(since,))
pitfalls: An interface over a leaky API is still leaky; the vendor's primitives propagate through the adapter unless it is written deliberately.
An abstraction layer is a new moving part: it raises onboarding cost and the chance of a systemic error, and it must earn its keep.
Choosing a third-party multi-cloud tool trades one vendor lock for another — count it, don't assume it removed one.
